claims.text: The target high-entropy alloys have varying compositions and structures.
Differences in alloy melting temperature can affect prediction accuracy.
BCC metals undergo a transition from an athermal plateau to strong temperature dependence.
The athermal-to-temperature-dependent transition occurs in BCC high-entropy alloys at approximately 0.4–0.5 Tm.
Incorporating melting-temperature differences and the BCC transition into a machine-learning model will aid prediction of melting temperature and other melting properties.
The model should be trained on a diverse dataset of high-entropy alloys.
The training data should span different melting temperatures and structures.
The machine-learning model will learn relationships among alloy composition, structure, and melting temperature.
Learned composition-structure-temperature relationships will enable predictions for unseen high-entropy alloys.
The proposed model will improve the accuracy of melting-temperature predictions relative to current capabilities.
The proposed model will improve the computational efficiency of melting-temperature predictions relative to current capabilities.
The model will also improve predictions of other, unspecified melting properties.
The model's validity is limited to high-entropy alloys with compositions and structures similar to those represented in its training data.
Complex composition-structure-melting-temperature relationships may create uncertainty in the model's predictions.
The model should be tested on alloys whose compositions and structures differ significantly from the training data.
Inaccurate predictions on substantially out-of-distribution alloys would show that the model is not generalizable.
Inaccurate predictions on substantially out-of-distribution alloys would falsify the stated hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The boundary restricts validity to alloys similar to the training data, whereas the proposed falsification test uses alloys significantly different from the training data and treats failure there as falsification. Poor out-of-distribution performance would not falsify the bounded in-domain claim.
